# The Book That Disagreed With Itself {#sec-the-book-that-disagreed-with-itself}

Mark is on chapter nine when Hal writes the sentence that ruins Tuesday.

"Grief," Hal writes, "is not something a person carries.
It is something a person builds, one room at a time, and lives inside."

It is a good sentence.
Mark rereads it twice, once for the rhythm and once to be sure, and it is only on the third pass that he remembers chapter two, where he wrote, in his own hand, that grief is exactly a thing a person carries, and that the whole tragedy of Aunt Ruth is that she never sets it down.

He opens chapter two to check.
He has not misremembered it.
Both sentences are still there, four hundred pages apart, and both of them are good, and Mark cannot tell you, at gunpoint, which one he believes.

"Cite chapter two," he tells Hal.

"Chapter two, page forty-one," Hal says.

Chapter two is thirty pages long.
Mark asks again, in case Hal misheard the question rather than invented the answer, and gets page sixty-three back, delivered with the same confidence, for the same sentence, in the same book.

He sends the draft to Em Dash anyway, because a book cannot be edited by a man arguing with himself in a document titled `untitled_final_v2`.
Em Dash returns it forty-one hours later.
She has added forty-one em-dashes and removed nothing.
Buried on page nine, one comment survives her pass intact: *your book has two opinions and no spine.*

Mark reads that sentence more times than he read Hal's.

He does the thing an editor's comment is supposed to make him do, which is stop rewriting sentences and start writing down what the sentences are for.
He opens a new file, plain text, no formatting Em Dash can improve.
Grief is a weight, not an architecture, he writes under a heading, and gives the heading a short name: `grief-weight`.
Underneath it he writes the sentence that has to be true for the rest of chapter two to stand.

By the end of the afternoon the file has six headings, six short names, and not one instance of the word "commitments," which Mark tried first and rejected because it sounded like a proposal he was not ready to make.
He calls them quirks instead.
A quirk is smaller than a belief and harder to walk back than a preference, which is exactly the size he needs.

He goes back to chapter nine and writes, above the paragraph Hal is about to ruin again, one line: *this chapter expresses grief-weight.* Hal reads it, and for the first time in nine chapters, agrees with chapter two.
